text_evidence.whisper_asr: This isn't magic. These are real small science experiments. Put two matches together and light them. The matches cling together like lovers, unwilling to separate. Add baking soda and an appropriate amount of white vinegar to a cup, and it will produce carbon dioxide. This invisible gas can actually extinguish a burning candle. This is the principle of a fire extinguisher. Fix an iron wire to both ends of a battery, attach a magnet, and then add a copper coil. The coil starts to spin. This is the working principle of a rotisserie oven. Rub a clove of garlic with your finger, and you can easily lift the egg yolk. This is an easy trick. Use garlic to draw a circle on the bottom of a pan, and the eggs you crack into it will be round. Wrap some cotton thread around a glass bottle a few times. Pour some alcohol onto the thread and light it with fire. After heating the bottle evenly by rotating it, quickly put it into cold water. You can then easily cut the glass bottle. Scrape off the red phosphorus from the match head with a small knife and pour it into the keyhole of a lock lock. Insert a match and light the match head. Wait for the match. The match to burn down to the red phosphorus inside the keyhole, and the lock with the lost key will open. Put leftover rainbow candy in a plate, arranging it in a circle. Pour a small amount of clear water into the center. You will see the beautiful rainbow slowly converge towards the middle. Cut a few slices into a chocolate bar, then subtly shift a piece like this. Suddenly, there's an extra piece. This way, you'll have endless chocolate to enjoy. Place a ping-pong ball on the air outlet of a hairdryer. You'll find that the ping-pong ball can actually float in the air. Even if you place two, they won't fall. This is Bernoulli's principle. Insert two pencils into salt water, connecting the tips to the positive and negative terminals of a 9-volt battery. You will see hydrogen and oxygen gas being generated in the water. This is the electrolysis effect. Place three bottle caps on a round magnet, then a plastic sheet. Rotate the gyroscope, slowly lift it, then slowly pull away the plastic sheet. The gyroscope will start to spin in midair. This is magnetic levitation. Place a lit candle in a basin of water, then invert a glass over it. The water from the basin will be... sucked into the glass. This is atmospheric pressure. Place a transparent cup in front of an arrow, and pour clear water into it. You will find that the arrow actually reverses direction. This is the principle of light refraction. Put frozen grapes into ice water, and the water will condense around the grapes. You now have the power to turn water into ice. Wrap an iron wire around two keys, aligning both ends with the positive and negative terminals of a battery. You have successfully made your own electric heating knife. This is the law of resistance. Shine a laser pointer onto clear water. You won't see the light passing through. Just add a small amount of milk to the water, and you'll see a clear path of light. This is the famous Tyndall effect. Form steel wool into a circle, place a phone in the middle, and make a call. The steel wool instantly sparks. This is the radiation from an incoming call on a phone. Pour sand into an electric hot plate, shake it gently, and place a magnetic steel ball on top. Turn on the power. You'll be surprised to find that the steel ball gains power and becomes an excellent painter. Put an egg into white vinegar, and after soaking overnight, take it out. Clean the surface, and you'll have a transparent and elastic skin egg. What do you do if a soda can tab breaks? Quickly rub the opening with a chopstick, and the soda can will open automatically. Do you know why this happens? Wrap a bamboo stick and a match head together in aluminum foil. Flatten the top. Rest it on the rim of a cup and light the match head. You can then simulate a rocket launch. Pour expired cooking oil into a cup. Add a little water, and then a few drops of food coloring. Drop in a few effervescent tablets. Next, you can enjoy the spectacular sight of an underwater volcano erupting. Place a ping-pong ball on the mouth of a water-filled bottle, then invert the bottle. The ping-pong ball surprisingly won't fall. This is atmospheric pressure. Intertwine two books together as if shuffling cards. The resulting friction can actually lift a large bucket of pure water. Tap the mouth of an empty bottle with a hammer, and the bottle won't break. But when we add a little water to the bottle and tap it gently, the bottle breaks. This is the famous water hammer effect. Dip a cotton swab in onion juice. And write words on a white paper. These words will only become visible after heating. This is the mystery of the book without words. On a standing piece of paper, a coin falls off as soon as you place it. If you first fold the paper to create a corner and place the coin on the corner, the coin will balance steadily on the paper. Even if you slowly unfold the paper, it won't fall. Bend toothpicks in the middle and arrange five of them as shown in the video. Drip a few drops of water in the middle, and the toothpicks will quietly gather to form a five-pointed star. This is water tension. If you're using a plastic sheet, you can use a transparent plastic sheet and cut four isosceles trapezoids, then glue them together with transparent tape. Make it into a funnel shape, place it on a phone, and play a 3D video. You have successfully made a simple naked-eye 3D projector. Science is ever-changing. Quickly try these experiments with your children. Let them put down their phones and fall in love with science.

Jobs have disappeared, young people are moving away, and nearly one percent of its population left in a single year. Number three, New York. Twelve percent of New Yorkers say it's the worst state to live in. Between rent prices that could fund a small nation and a pace that burns you out before you turn 30, who can blame them? At number two, New Jersey. Ten percent of residents call it the worst state in America because of traffic jams, high property taxes, and an unshakable reputation for being the loud neighbor. And finally, the state most hated by its own people, where one in four residents say it's the worst place to live. That state is Illinois.

text_evidence.whisper_asr: Could the forbidden fruit from the tree of knowledge in the Bible be psychedelic mushrooms? Because in nature, fungus are the only quote-unquote tree capable of permanently altering the way the human brain works. This happens because mushrooms can activate neurogenesis, which is the formation of new neurons. The stoned ape theory is based on this and proposes that cavemen or early humans started eating psychedelic mushrooms as part of their diet. This led to increased intelligence, creativity, and consciousness. Mushrooms also serve the same reproductive purpose as the fruit from plants and are even referred to as fruiting bodies in science. But instead of seeds, they produce spores. So not only do psychedelic mushrooms alter the brain like the forbidden fruit Adam and Eve ate, but they also act as the actual fruit of the fungus. While the fungus itself, which is its underground mycelium, acts as the plant or drug. The fungus is also known as the tree of knowledge. Even more interesting, this tree ironically bears a striking resemblance to the nerves of our brains and bodies, which function in the same way. As fungal mycelium and nerves both process and transport electrical information, aka knowledge. Also, ancient Sumerians and Mesoamericans called mushrooms the flesh of the gods and believed that mushrooms connected humans to divine realms. All across the world, from Europe to India to China. Ancient cultures considered mushrooms to be sacred and a path to higher consciousness. With all this in mind, could fungus be the tree of knowledge and mushrooms the forbidden fruit of the Bible? Comment to let me know what you think.

text_evidence.whisper_asr: Opioid use disorder among veterans and first responders is a growing public health concern shaped by the demands of service. Combat exposure, emergency response, and repeated encounters with injury and loss place heavy physical and psychological strain on these professionals. Many develop chronic pain from injuries, surgeries, or line-of-duty trauma, often beginning with prescribed opioids that can progress to dependence over time. Co-occurring conditions such as PTSD, depression, anxiety, and sleep disorders further increased risk. Opioids may temporarily relieve both physical and emotional pain, reinforcing use during stressful transitions like returning from deployment or retiring from service. Stigma within military and emergency cultures, where strength and self-reliance are emphasized, often delays help-seeking. Barriers to care include fear of career consequences, limited access to specialized treatment, and fragmented transitions between service and civilian health care. These gaps raise overdose risk, especially during isolation or reduced tolerance. Effective treatment is well-established. Medications for opioid use disorder combined with trauma-informed therapy, peer support, pain management alternatives, and integrated mental health care significantly improve outcomes. Supporting recovery honors service, protects families, and strengthens communities.

Ti wo ata wakon, te ma joba she life, te jo maru dwe lejo. O tobe o ju be lo ko dah si disi yon lo ju. Fala no, bo ti e. Kalo man bo ti e to shora e, to ba business si yon lo, to tabeshi ti to wata. To ba ti e lo, she bi ko bada. Ojo lojo kini ano, ti an, si mami yire. Tenye le ni loba alayo yon, to loba pisili ayo. Ti wata, ti e, te bere sin she life, to lo wa classless. Nambago e kwa walo soro ju, lo ri life unye o. I walo nimbo celebrity ni nao, ye koma pake jaran, we wo picture to poster, wo bo she reo daran, wo she go, mo ule maskini record life unye, ni tori moni nkote mi faye mi she, mo she in struggle ati jenyon. Bo mo comment lo u life unye, mo sakwa e dwe lejo to onro, yoshi ma kwa da, pae lo jo kon, oblo kimi, abo oblo kimi. Oli yoda account mi ni do, bo, shori toba dah si disi yelo ju, wala e onkweni. Oma unweni, ye oma lo si police station, obo ujo e ti bache, o ti bache, kosi koto ma chesi. To be honest, wa don't want to sound insensitive. Nik ba tenye bak kwe jok po, te ba onro, ujwe lejo, nik ba tenye wan sheti, ni fun e ba, tenye wan sheti, e fun e ba, e kwe yoko kailara. Wala e uye kogbojusi le. Atojwa ti moti mokwe, i wata, wan te jaman kura yin kiri, ari teni mo, uwi ya fakpa di boti se, mo lele imejeji. Ni bo boni, atojwa yon moti dey. Omo, atoja bala, atoja ansi, e wan kosho yon lori life unye, borara, o proof i pwe mo, ofile si jwe le. E o, a muda kodja lori yon yoti, o feko muda kodja lori yon unye. Ni si ba yon kailara, yon she video. Mo, moti rini yori, rana mati fe erito ten videos, to ti she. O paniki, kwe yako paniki. A wato rojo ti, wato ba yako paniki, lojo kini agon, shorobo ma bombe eni. Bo she paniki, yoko mbimi nuni, like, ah, mi monotu mo vi legba, si mo, mi ole block yetori, mo fe maria, mo ori buru kuto onye sitori. O gudo shi kwe leko, um, shi pa da pae, to ba, to ba pa da len, bo she mind business ye. Kota be shi to, wa yi wata jeje, kota. Eh, iwa mbawi, and I just hope that you see this video, so da wa len, be yon she ma mind business ye, yon kis kote, yon yon yon man soro si. A lejo wa lori black hapu yi, oni karuku levo, oni karuku yato siramu. Levo, oni karuku yato black hapu, loko ogu aku. Even though, o shi la unkoto lewo ju, kosiyaniti wo, wale, le soro si, kosiyaniti wo le be, kosiyaniti wo le tebu mata e, kilo le to be. Eh? I re fun e.

text_evidence.whisper_asr: Opioid use disorder is a treatable medical condition, yet access to evidence-based care remains unequal. Medications such as buprenorphine, methadone, and naltrexone reduce overdose risk and improve recovery, but many people never receive them due to systemic barriers. Racial and ethnic disparities persist across treatment systems. Communities of color are less likely to receive medication-based care and more likely to face punitive responses instead of treatment. Rural communities encounter additional challenges, including provider shortages, long travel distances, limited transportation, and fewer treatment programs. Socioeconomic factors further widen gaps. People without stable housing, insurance, or employment often struggle to access consistent care. Limited clinic hours, prior authorization required, and poorly coordinated transitions such as after-hospital discharge or release from incarceration create dangerous interruptions in treatment. Stigma remains a significant barrier, discouraging both patients and providers from engaging in care. Reducing disparities requires policy reform, workforce expansion, culturally responsive care, and integration of addiction treatment into primary care, emergency departments, and community settings. Closing these gaps is essential to saving lives and achieving health equity.

text_evidence.whisper_asr: Legal barriers continue to limit access to evidence-based opioid addiction treatment. Restrictive regulations around medications for opioid use disorder have reduced the number of clinicians able or willing to provide care, especially in primary care and rural settings. Although some rules have eased, regulatory complexity still discourages participation. Criminalization also creates significant barriers. Many individuals fear arrest, incarceration, or loss of child custody if they seek help. Mandatory reporting, probation requirements, and drug-related arrests disrupt treatment continuity. Incarceration without access to medication treatment increases overdose risk after release due to reduced tolerance. Insurance and policy gaps further delay care. Prior authorization requirements, coverage limits, and inconsistent Medicaid expansion prevent timely treatment during high-risk periods. Separation between addiction treatment and generalization. In addition to the need for medical care, fragments care and complicates coordination. Zoning laws and community opposition can also block treatment centers and harm reduction services. text_evidence.whisper_asr: student just defied you publicly and to get them to stop, you previewed consequences. But the situation got worse and not better. Here's why. My name is Rashonda Glenn. I have been a teacher for 29 years and I've spent the last 18 years teaching students with severe behavior challenges. So when I say previewing consequences, I mean that you gave a warning to the student about a punishment that they will receive if they don't do something that you've asked them to do. It sounds like this. If you don't sit down right now, you're going to the office. This is your last warning. Keep it up and you'll lose recess. The reason that previewing consequences escalates the situation is because it turns the moment into a power struggle. And students with a history of behavior challenges will experience these warnings as threats. And in front of their peers, they'll feel pressure to prove that they're not intimidated by them. Now the focus is going to shift away from the behavior and onto the fight for control of the moment. Instead of threats, or warnings, pause first, regulate yourself, and then calmly give the student a clear instruction. Then let your track record win the moment. Yes, the other students will begin watching and they may even begin giggling. It is public defiance. Being watched by the class actually puts pressure on us and makes us feel like we must respond with control. But students also pay attention to our patterns. If we have a history of being fair and consistent, the other students already know how this situation is going to end. So they will either disengage or they'll come to your defense. Public defiance makes us feel like we have to do something special to win the moment, without realizing that our track record has already done the work for us. And that leads to the most important question of all. If responding with control isn't the answer, well, how do we respond? If you want a clear, step-by-step framework for handling public defiance from students, Without losing authority, I break down my full seven-step approach on my brand new YouTube channel. Yay! Just click the link in my bio to watch the full video.

text_evidence.whisper_asr: Is it flu or is it COVID? Doctors say one symptom can help you tell the difference. It's winter and suddenly everyone at work is working from home, but not all winter bugs are the same. GP Rupert Palmer says there is a key giveaway and it's all about the cough. Doctors say a COVID cough is dry and persistent, often lingering longer than flu. The NHS defines it as coughing nonstop for more than an hour or having three or more coughing fits in a day, even after other symptoms start to fade. Many people recover within a few weeks, but some take longer and not everyone needs to take a COVID test anymore. text_evidence.whisper_asr: Most freshmen fail their first semester of college because they don't know this one thing. College learning is completely different from high school learning, and if you don't adjust yourself well, you're going to crash and burn. High school rewards memorization and repetition, and college demands analysis, understanding, and application. If you study the same way you did before, it'll be too late before you realize that you don't remember anything you studied. The shift isn't about studying harder. It's about understanding that college tests how you think and not just what you remember. There are three parts to college learning that you must understand so that you can be well-prepared. Number one, memorization doesn't work for college exams. High school tests are straightforward, but college wants you to analyze concepts, connect ideas across topics, and apply knowledge to new situations. You need active recall. Number two, no one will hold your hand. High school teachers remind you about assignments daily and give you study guides. Professors hand you a syllabus on day one and expect you to manage everything yourself. You need a system that tracks what you've mastered and what still needs work. Number three, the volume is overwhelming. One college class covers what used to be a full semester in high school. You'll be reading entire textbooks in two weeks. You can't study everything. You need to break material into learning objectives and focus on what actually matters for the exam. Here's how to handle it. All three challenges systematically. First, outline your learning objectives using the syllabus or learning guide that your professor provided you with. Gather everything like lecture slides, notes, PDFs. You'll need to meet each objective. Assign everything to the respective goal. Upload all of it to studiesmart.ai. AI extracts key concepts and generates questions automatically. Next, use active recall by clicking on hidden keywords, which you know, and typing out the ones that you don't. If you're still not sure, explain the concept to AI and get feedback. Retention scores keep track of your memory. When any topic falls below 80%, review it right away. Finally, take AI-generated practice. Test in multiple formats. MCQs, open-ended, true-false, verbal. Don't study like it's high school. Try studiesmart.ai risk-free today.

properties.name: LSD
properties.pharmacology: Serotonin receptor agonist (5-HT2A); psychedelic; Hallucinogen acting on serotonin receptors.
properties.effects: Hallucinations; altered perception; euphoria; mood changes; anxiety; paranoia; flashbacks.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low physical toxicity; psychological risks (bad trips; psychosis); Psychological distress; accidents; potential persistent psychosis.

properties.name: Marijuana\Cannabis
properties.pharmacology: Contains THC; a psychoactive cannabinoid. Smoked; ingested; or vaped. Acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain.; Contains THC acting on cannabinoid receptors.
properties.effects: Euphoria; relaxation; altered sensory perception; impaired memory; and coordination. Can cause anxiety or paranoia in high doses.; Relaxation; euphoria; altered perception; anxiety; paranoia; impaired memory.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; overdose is rare but can cause acute psychosis or anxiety. Chronic use may impair cognitive function; especially in adolescents. Risk of dependency.; Dependence; respiratory issues (smoking); cognitive impairment; psychosis (high doses).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use federally; though legal in some states for medical/recreational use).; Varies by state (USA); Schedule I (federal)
properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.name: Crack Cocaine
properties.pharmacology: Smokable cocaine form rapidly increasing dopamine levels.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; increased energy; alertness; paranoia; aggression; cardiovascular issues.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Addiction; psychosis; cardiovascular complications; respiratory issues.

properties.name: Acetaminophen and Oxycodone (Percocet®)
properties.pharmacology: Combination of oxycodone (opioid) and acetaminophen (non-opioid analgesic). Oxycodone binds to opioid receptors; acetaminophen inhibits prostaglandin production.
properties.effects: Pain relief; sedation; euphoria; respiratory depression; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Liver damage (acetaminophen overdose); opioid dependence; addiction; respiratory depression.

properties.name: para-Fluorofentanyl
properties.pharmacology: Synthetic opioid; mu-opioid agonist
properties.effects: Similar to fentanyl: euphoria; sedation
properties.toxicity_and_harm: High overdose risk; untested safety profile

properties.name: delta-9-THC-COOH
properties.pharmacology: Inactive metabolite
properties.effects: None (metabolite)
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; indicates cannabis use
properties.legal_status: Varies (cannabis legal in some US states; illegal federally)

properties.name: delta-9-THC-COOH
properties.pharmacology: Inactive metabolite
properties.effects: None (metabolite)
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; indicates cannabis use
properties.legal_status: Varies (cannabis legal in some US states; illegal federally)

properties.name: Marijuana\Cannabis
properties.pharmacology: Contains THC; a psychoactive cannabinoid. Smoked; ingested; or vaped. Acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain.; Contains THC acting on cannabinoid receptors.
properties.effects: Euphoria; relaxation; altered sensory perception; impaired memory; and coordination. Can cause anxiety or paranoia in high doses.; Relaxation; euphoria; altered perception; anxiety; paranoia; impaired memory.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; overdose is rare but can cause acute psychosis or anxiety. Chronic use may impair cognitive function; especially in adolescents. Risk of dependency.; Dependence; respiratory issues (smoking); cognitive impairment; psychosis (high doses).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use federally; though legal in some states for medical/recreational use).; Varies by state (USA); Schedule I (federal)
properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.name: Crack Cocaine
properties.pharmacology: Smokable cocaine form rapidly increasing dopamine levels.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; increased energy; alertness; paranoia; aggression; cardiovascular issues.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Addiction; psychosis; cardiovascular complications; respiratory issues.

properties.name: Heroin
properties.pharmacology: Opioid derived from morphine; a natural opium poppy product. Binds to opioid receptors; producing analgesia and euphoria. Administered by injection; snorting; or smoking.; Prodrug to morphine; Âµ-opioid agonist; µ-opioid agonist; binding to opioid receptors.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; sedation; pain relief; followed by drowsiness and mental clouding. Can cause respiratory depression and constipation.; Euphoria; 'rush'; respiratory depression; Pain relief; euphoria; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Extremely addictive; overdose can lead to fatal respiratory depression. High risk of hepatitis or HIV from shared needles. 80% of users start with prescription opioids.; High overdose; respiratory depression; infection risk; Addiction; overdose; death; infectious diseases (injection).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use; high abuse potential).; Schedule I; Schedule I (USA)

properties.name: MDA
properties.pharmacology: Serotonin/dopamine releaser; empathogen
properties.effects: Euphoria; empathy; mild hallucinations
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Similar to MDMA: neurotoxicity; hyperthermia

properties.name: MDMA (Ecstasy)
properties.pharmacology: Empathogen‑stimulant (increases serotonin; dopamine; norepinephrine release)
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (DEA Diversion Control Division; Rosalind Franklin University)

properties.name: Oxazepam
properties.pharmacology: Benzodiazepine; GABA-A receptor agonist
properties.effects: Anxiolytic; sedation
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; withdrawal; lower overdose risk

properties.name: Phencyclidine (PCP)
properties.pharmacology: NMDA receptor antagonist; dissociative
properties.effects: Dissociation; hallucinations; aggression
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Psychosis; neurotoxicity; violent behavior

properties.name: LSD
properties.pharmacology: Serotonin receptor agonist (5-HT2A); psychedelic; Hallucinogen acting on serotonin receptors.
properties.effects: Hallucinations; altered perception; euphoria; mood changes; anxiety; paranoia; flashbacks.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low physical toxicity; psychological risks (bad trips; psychosis); Psychological distress; accidents; potential persistent psychosis.

properties.name: Promethazine
properties.pharmacology: Antihistamine blocking histamine receptors.
properties.effects: Reduced allergy symptoms; sedation; anti-nausea; drowsiness; dizziness; dry mouth.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; overdose (with depressants); respiratory depression.

properties.name: Heroin
properties.pharmacology: Opioid derived from morphine; a natural opium poppy product. Binds to opioid receptors; producing analgesia and euphoria. Administered by injection; snorting; or smoking.; Prodrug to morphine; Âµ-opioid agonist; µ-opioid agonist; binding to opioid receptors.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; sedation; pain relief; followed by drowsiness and mental clouding. Can cause respiratory depression and constipation.; Euphoria; 'rush'; respiratory depression; Pain relief; euphoria; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Extremely addictive; overdose can lead to fatal respiratory depression. High risk of hepatitis or HIV from shared needles. 80% of users start with prescription opioids.; High overdose; respiratory depression; infection risk; Addiction; overdose; death; infectious diseases (injection).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use; high abuse potential).; Schedule I; Schedule I (USA)

properties.name: MDMA (Ecstasy)
properties.pharmacology: Empathogen‑stimulant (increases serotonin; dopamine; norepinephrine release)
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (DEA Diversion Control Division; Rosalind Franklin University)

properties.name: LSD

properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.toxicity_and_harm: Addiction; psychosis; cardiovascular complications; respiratory issues.

properties.name: LSD
properties.pharmacology: Serotonin receptor agonist (5-HT2A); psychedelic; Hallucinogen acting on serotonin receptors.
properties.effects: Hallucinations; altered perception; euphoria; mood changes; anxiety; paranoia; flashbacks.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low physical toxicity; psychological risks (bad trips; psychosis); Psychological distress; accidents; potential persistent psychosis.

properties.name: Acetaminophen and Oxycodone (Percocet®)
properties.pharmacology: Combination of oxycodone (opioid) and acetaminophen (non-opioid analgesic). Oxycodone binds to opioid receptors; acetaminophen inhibits prostaglandin production.
properties.effects: Pain relief; sedation; euphoria; respiratory depression; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Liver damage (acetaminophen overdose); opioid dependence; addiction; respiratory depression.

properties.name: Promethazine
properties.pharmacology: Antihistamine blocking histamine receptors.
properties.effects: Reduced allergy symptoms; sedation; anti-nausea; drowsiness; dizziness; dry mouth.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; overdose (with depressants); respiratory depression.

properties.name: LSD

properties.toxicity_and_harm: Addiction; psychosis; cardiovascular complications; respiratory issues.

properties.pharmacology: Inactive metabolite

properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; indicates cannabis use

properties.name: Marijuana\Cannabis
properties.pharmacology: Contains THC; a psychoactive cannabinoid. Smoked; ingested; or vaped. Acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain.; Contains THC acting on cannabinoid receptors.
properties.effects: Euphoria; relaxation; altered sensory perception; impaired memory; and coordination. Can cause anxiety or paranoia in high doses.; Relaxation; euphoria; altered perception; anxiety; paranoia; impaired memory.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; overdose is rare but can cause acute psychosis or anxiety. Chronic use may impair cognitive function; especially in adolescents. Risk of dependency.; Dependence; respiratory issues (smoking); cognitive impairment; psychosis (high doses).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use federally; though legal in some states for medical/recreational use).; Varies by state (USA); Schedule I (federal)
properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.name: Crack Cocaine
properties.pharmacology: Smokable cocaine form rapidly increasing dopamine levels.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; increased energy; alertness; paranoia; aggression; cardiovascular issues.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Addiction; psychosis; cardiovascular complications; respiratory issues.

properties.name: Heroin

properties.effects: Intense euphoria; sedation; pain relief; followed by drowsiness and mental clouding. Can cause respiratory depression and constipation.; Euphoria; 'rush'; respiratory depression; Pain relief; euphoria; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Extremely addictive; overdose can lead to fatal respiratory depression. properties.name: Alprazolam (Xanax®)
properties.pharmacology: Benzodiazepine enhancing GABA activity; producing a calming effect.
properties.effects: Reduced anxiety; sedation; muscle relaxation; drowsiness; dizziness; impaired coordination.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; withdrawal symptoms; overdose risk (with depressants); cognitive impairment.

properties.name: Marijuana\Cannabis
properties.pharmacology: Contains THC; a psychoactive cannabinoid. Smoked; ingested; or vaped. Acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain.; Contains THC acting on cannabinoid receptors.
properties.effects: Euphoria; relaxation; altered sensory perception; impaired memory; and coordination. Can cause anxiety or paranoia in high doses.; Relaxation; euphoria; altered perception; anxiety; paranoia; impaired memory.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; overdose is rare but can cause acute psychosis or anxiety. Chronic use may impair cognitive function; especially in adolescents. Risk of dependency.; Dependence; respiratory issues (smoking); cognitive impairment; psychosis (high doses).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use federally; though legal in some states for medical/recreational use).; Varies by state (USA); Schedule I (federal)
properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.name: GHB
properties.pharmacology: Depressant acting on the central nervous system; causing sedation and euphoria.
properties.effects: Sedation; euphoria; disinhibition; nausea; vomiting; respiratory depression.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; withdrawal symptoms; overdose; coma; death.

properties.name: Steroids
properties.pharmacology: Synthetic substances mimicking testosterone; promoting muscle growth.
properties.effects: Increased muscle mass; strength; aggression; acne; liver damage; cardiovascular issues.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; hormonal imbalances; psychiatric disorders; cardiovascular complications.

properties.name: Marijuana Concentrates
properties.pharmacology: High-THC extracts from marijuana.

properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; respiratory issues; cognitive impairment; psychosis.; psychosis; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).
properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.name: delta-9-THC-COOH
properties.pharmacology: Inactive metabolite
properties.effects: None (metabolite)
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; indicates cannabis use
properties.legal_status: Varies (cannabis legal in some US states; illegal federally)

properties.name: Marijuana\Cannabis
properties.pharmacology: Contains THC; a psychoactive cannabinoid. Smoked; ingested; or vaped. Acts on cannabinoid receptors in the brain.; Contains THC acting on cannabinoid receptors.
properties.effects: Euphoria; relaxation; altered sensory perception; impaired memory; and coordination. Can cause anxiety or paranoia in high doses.; Relaxation; euphoria; altered perception; anxiety; paranoia; impaired memory.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; overdose is rare but can cause acute psychosis or anxiety. Chronic use may impair cognitive function; especially in adolescents. Risk of dependency.; Dependence; respiratory issues (smoking); cognitive impairment; psychosis (high doses).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use federally; though legal in some states for medical/recreational use).; Varies by state (USA); Schedule I (federal)
properties.pubchem_cid: Dependence; addiction; overdose; liver damage (with acetaminophen).

properties.name: Crack Cocaine
properties.pharmacology: Smokable cocaine form rapidly increasing dopamine levels.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; increased energy; alertness; paranoia; aggression; cardiovascular issues.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Addiction; psychosis; cardiovascular complications; respiratory issues.

properties.name: Heroin
properties.pharmacology: Opioid derived from morphine; a natural opium poppy product. Binds to opioid receptors; producing analgesia and euphoria. Administered by injection; snorting; or smoking.; Prodrug to morphine; Âµ-opioid agonist; µ-opioid agonist; binding to opioid receptors.
properties.effects: Intense euphoria; sedation; pain relief; followed by drowsiness and mental clouding. Can cause respiratory depression and constipation.; Euphoria; 'rush'; respiratory depression; Pain relief; euphoria; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Extremely addictive; overdose can lead to fatal respiratory depression. High risk of hepatitis or HIV from shared needles. 80% of users start with prescription opioids.; High overdose; respiratory depression; infection risk; Addiction; overdose; death; infectious diseases (injection).
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (no accepted medical use; high abuse potential).; Schedule I; Schedule I (USA)

properties.name: MDA
properties.pharmacology: Serotonin/dopamine releaser; empathogen
properties.effects: Euphoria; empathy; mild hallucinations
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Similar to MDMA: neurotoxicity; hyperthermia

properties.name: MDMA (Ecstasy)
properties.pharmacology: Empathogen‑stimulant (increases serotonin; dopamine; norepinephrine release)
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (DEA Diversion Control Division; Rosalind Franklin University)

properties.name: Oxazepam
properties.pharmacology: Benzodiazepine; GABA-A receptor agonist
properties.effects: Anxiolytic; sedation
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; withdrawal; lower overdose risk

properties.name: Phencyclidine (PCP)
properties.pharmacology: NMDA receptor antagonist; dissociative
properties.effects: Dissociation; hallucinations; aggression
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Psychosis; neurotoxicity; violent behavior

properties.name: Acetaminophen and Oxycodone (Percocet®)
properties.pharmacology: Combination of oxycodone (opioid) and acetaminophen (non-opioid analgesic). Oxycodone binds to opioid receptors; acetaminophen inhibits prostaglandin production.
properties.effects: Pain relief; sedation; euphoria; respiratory depression; constipation; nausea.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Liver damage (acetaminophen overdose); opioid dependence; addiction; respiratory depression.

properties.name: delta-9-THC-COOH
properties.pharmacology: Inactive metabolite
properties.effects: None (metabolite)
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Low toxicity; indicates cannabis use
properties.legal_status: Varies (cannabis legal in some US states; illegal federally)

properties.name: Ketamine
properties.pharmacology: Dissociative anesthetic blocking NMDA receptors.
properties.effects: Dissociation; hallucinations; analgesia; confusion; agitation; cardiovascular issues.
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; bladder damage; cognitive impairment; accidents.

properties.name: MDMA (Ecstasy)
properties.pharmacology: Empathogen‑stimulant (increases serotonin; dopamine; norepinephrine release)
properties.legal_status: Schedule I (DEA Diversion Control Division; Rosalind Franklin University)

properties.name: Oxazepam
properties.pharmacology: Benzodiazepine; GABA-A receptor agonist
properties.effects: Anxiolytic; sedation
properties.toxicity_and_harm: Dependence; withdrawal; lower overdose risk
